title_ar: إذا قرئ القرآن بحضرة أحد هل يلزمه الإنصات له ؟
title_en: If the Qur'an Is Recited in Someone's Presence, Is He Obliged to Listen in Silence?
body_ar: أجمع المفسرون على أن قول الله تعالى ( و إذا قرئ القرآن فاستمعوا له و أنصتوا ) أن المقصود قراءته في الصلاة أي قراءة الإمام. أما في غير ذلك فلا يجب الاستماع له لكنه مندوب و له نصف أجر القراءة
body_en: The exegetes are in consensus that the words of God, be He exalted, {And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent} (Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:204), mean its recitation in the prayer — that is, the imam's recitation. As for other than that, listening to it is not obligatory (wājib), but it is recommended (mandūb), and the listener has half the reward of the one reciting.

flags.context: the opening claim of the answer
options: the exegetes are of one view
flags.note: Recorded exactly as given. This is a claim of scholarly consensus (ijmāʿ) among the exegetes on the referent of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:204, made without citation. It is not softened to 'most' or 'the exegetes generally', and no authority has been supplied for it.

options: the listener has half the reward of the one reciting
he has half the reward of the recitation
flags.note: The pronoun is unmarked; the subject of the sentence is the listener, so the reward is his. Stated without a supporting text; none has been added.

translator_notes: The same verse is quoted by the questioner in record 892 of this slice, which is about reciting behind the imam. The two records are answering related questions from opposite directions and should be read together, though the Sheikh does not cross-refer.
The ruling terms are the fixed renderings: not obligatory (wājib), but recommended (mandūb).
The source puts the Qur'anic text in ordinary round brackets; the English uses the corpus convention. Qur'anic renderings are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic.
